_experiment: CAPACITY A/B (2026-08-15, RL_METHODOLOGY_PLAN.md section 1A.14). Exactly ONE variable differs from run_default.json: trunk_hidden (128,128) -> (512,512), the TRAINABLE per-deck DeckNetwork trunk. 82,877 -> 515,261 params, 6.2x. Everything else copied verbatim, including ppo (this arm inherits PPO_DEFAULTS, which now carries lr=2e-4).
_why:
Section 1A.13 established that the late-training plateau is NOT a trust-region problem: lr=2e-4 eliminated KL truncation outright (99% -> 6% of updates) and still plateaued and oscillated exactly as 3e-4 did, reaching baseline-final strength by ~4,000 games/deck and then flat. Four optimizer-level mechanisms are now falsified by measurement -- entropy, advantage scale, Adam-step count, and the trust region itself. What has never been tested is whether the model can represent a better policy at all.

The split is stark: the frozen SetTransformer encoder is 117,056 params and the trainable per-deck trunk is 82,877, so 59% of the model is frozen at whatever 500 games/deck of near-random pretrain play produced, and the trainable half is small. This arm scales the trainable half, which is the cheap half to test.
_why_this_before_the_frozen_encoder: The encoder is the more interesting suspect -- it was frozen after 500 games/deck of weak play and has never seen the state distribution the agents now inhabit. But testing it costs a full pretrain cycle (~5h) or a real code change: the stack is shared across four per-deck Adam optimizers, so making it trainable means four optimizers mutating the same tensors with independent momentum, which is a design question and not a flag. The trunk needs neither -- d_model is unchanged, so the frozen-stack interface is untouched, and a fresh league now reaches its plateau in ~4,000 games (~70 min). If 6.2x trainable capacity does not move the plateau, capacity is ruled out and the encoder becomes the prime suspect by elimination, which is how the last four mechanisms were resolved.
_why_wide_not_deep: (512,512) rather than (256,256,256) at similar parameter count: the trunk activation is Tanh, and deeper Tanh stacks train worse (vanishing gradients), so depth would confound a capacity result with an optimization one. Width is the cleaner test.
_success_criterion: PRE-REGISTERED, judge against these and do not move them afterward. (1) THE PLATEAU: does vs_gauntlet against the fixed reference (baseline live @20,016) keep RISING past cum ~4,000, where every run so far has gone flat? Judge the TRAJECTORY across all sampled points, never a single reading -- section 1A.13 had to withdraw a headline for exactly that error, and section 1A.7 before it. (2) LEVEL: does the trajectory's late plateau sit meaningfully above the ~51% band that lr=2e-4 settled into? (3) NULL RESULT IS INFORMATIVE AND MUST BE REPORTED AS SUCH: if 6.2x capacity changes nothing, capacity is not the ceiling, and the frozen encoder plus the meta's own structure (section 1A.5) are what remain.
_stop_at: 8,000 games/deck, not the 10,000 the lr arms used. Rationale: a 6.2x larger trunk may simply need more games to converge, which would masquerade as 'capacity did not help', so the run must go comfortably past the ~4,000 plateau point to distinguish the two -- but the lr trajectory showed nothing new after ~6,000, so 8,000 is enough and 20,000 would be waste.
_gauntlet_note: Points at the 20,016-game baseline, same fixed reference every other arm used, so the trajectories are directly comparable across arms. Budget-confounded in the baseline's favour and reads low by construction; the comparison ACROSS arms is what matters, not the absolute number. Cross-league loading is safe at a different trunk width because _run_eval_vs_gauntlet now reads the gauntlet's own width off its checkpoint (rl.checkpoint.trunk_hidden_from_deck_checkpoint) rather than assuming the running league's.
